lesson.title: The Three-Part Test for a GPT
lesson.summary: This section unpacks the three concrete criteria economists use to test whether a technology qualifies as a General Purpose Technology, explaining the mechanism behind each one with historical examples.
lesson.body:
You already know that a General Purpose Technology is something that reshapes the economy the way electricity or the steam engine did, rather than staying confined to one industry. But "reshapes the economy" is vague enough to argue about endlessly. To make the label useful, economists turned it into a checklist: three specific traits a technology has to show before you're allowed to call it general purpose.

The first trait is that the technology has to function as an input into many different, unrelated kinds of production, not just one. Think about why this matters mechanically: an invention that only helps bakers bake bread affects one sector's costs and output. Electricity, by contrast, could power a textile loom, run a hospital's refrigeration, drive a streetcar, and light an office, all using the same underlying physical principle wired into different machines. That breadth is what lets a technology move the productivity of an entire economy rather than a single niche.

The second trait is that the technology keeps getting better and cheaper over time, rather than arriving fully formed and then stagnating. This matters because adoption is an economic decision ,  businesses only switch to a new technology when the switching cost is justified by the payoff, and that calculation only keeps improving for buyers if the underlying technology itself keeps improving. Early electric generators were inefficient and expensive to install; later refinements in generation, transmission, and motor design steadily lowered the cost of using electric power, which is part of why adoption spread from a handful of factories to nearly every building over the following decades. A one-time invention that never gets refined can't sustain that kind of expanding uptake.

The third trait is the ability to spark complementary innovation ,  new products, tools, and even new ways of organizing a business that only became possible, or only became worthwhile, once the core technology existed. This is a different mechanism from the first two: it's not about the technology itself getting used more places or getting cheaper, it's about it becoming a platform other people build on top of. Electric power didn't just replace steam engines with electric motors doing the same job; it enabled factories to be redesigned entirely, since machines no longer needed to be arranged around a central steam shaft and could instead be laid out according to the logic of the production process itself. That reorganization was a downstream innovation that electricity made possible but didn't itself invent.

Notice that these three tests are independent of each other ,  a technology could satisfy one or two without satisfying all three, and the label "general purpose" is meant to be reserved for the rare cases that clear all three bars simultaneously. That's the point of turning a fuzzy, impressive-sounding idea into a checklist: it stops "general purpose" from being a compliment you hand out to any technology you find exciting, and turns it into something you can actually check a given technology against, one criterion at a time.
